title: Go channels: the hchan struct and lock-based design
prerequisites: Understanding of mutexes and condition variables

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A channel is a post office with one delivery window. People drop letters in the box (send) and pick letters up (receive). The post office has a strict rule: if you come to send and the box is full, you sit in a waiting chair until a spot opens; if you come to pick and the box is empty, you sit until a letter arrives. The postmaster (a lock) makes sure only one person touches the box at a time. Everyone waiting gets called in the order they sat down (FIFO), so no one is ever skipped.
progressiveExplaining.junior: ch := make(chan int, 3) creates a buffered channel. Sends and receives block when the buffer is full/empty respectively; unbuffered channels (make(chan int)) block until the other side is ready, making them synchronization points. close(ch) signals 'no more sends'; ranging (for v := range ch) drains until close. The primary use cases: hand-off synchronization between goroutines, work queues (buffered channels + workers), and graceful shutdown signals (close(ch) as a broadcast). select multiplexes over multiple channels: select { case v := <-ch1: ...; case ch2 <- v: ...; default: ... }.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, channels are the 'communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating' primitive. The runtime implements each channel as an hchan struct guarded by a mutex, with FIFO wait queues of blocked senders and receivers. When a send finds a waiting receiver, the value is handed off directly (no buffering hop); otherwise it goes into the ring buffer. Because every operation takes the channel's lock, unbuffered handoffs and hot buffered channels serialize on the lock — throughput-wise they are closer to a mutex + condition variable than to a lock-free queue. The design choice is deliberate: simplicity and correctness over raw speed. select is implemented by locking all involved channels and randomly ordering the cases to avoid starvation.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: hchan contains: qcount, dataqsiz, buf (ring buffer pointer), elemsize, closed, sendx/recvx (ring indices), sendq/recvq (wait queues of sudog nodes), and a lock (mutex). chansend/chansend1: lock the channel; if a sudog is parked in recvq, dequeue it, copy the value directly into the receiver's stack slot, and wake the goroutine (no buffer involved); else if qcount < dataqsiz, write into the ring buffer; else park the sender by creating a sudog, pushing it into sendq, and gopark (the G parks, the M is released). chanrecv mirrors the logic and handles closed channels by returning the zero value. Buffered channels with a mutex perform contended operations at memory-sync cost; select uses fastpath for single-case and selectgo otherwise, locking channels in order, registering the goroutine on all, and waiting via a common wait mechanism.

codeComparison.title: Unbuffered handoff vs buffered work queue
codeComparison.summary: Unbuffered channels synchronize two goroutines with a rendezvous; buffered channels decouple producers from workers and need explicit close for completion.

legacyOrBad.label: Unbuffered broadcast (blocking main)
legacyOrBad.snippet:
done := make(chan struct{})
go func() { work(); done <- struct{}{} }()
<-done // blocks until the goroutine sends

modernOrGood.label: Buffered queue + close broadcast
modernOrGood.snippet:
jobs := make(chan int, 10)
// N workers; close(jobs) broadcasts completion, workers drain

interviewGotchas.question: Why is a buffered channel more like a mutex than a lock-free queue under the hood?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This distinguishes candidates who assume channels are high-performance lock-free queues from those who know the runtime's actual design and its implications.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Every hchan operation takes the channel's mutex (hchan.lock) — sends, receives, and close all serialize on it. So a hot buffered channel is contended the way a mutex-protected queue is: throughput is bounded by lock hold time and cache-line bouncing, not by lock-free atomics. The runtime chose this for correctness and simplicity: FIFO order is guaranteed by the wait queues, memory ordering is handled by the lock, and the ring buffer keeps buffer management trivial. The practical implication: for very high-throughput work distribution, a hand-rolled sharded queue or Go 1.22+ iterators/slice-based pools can beat a single channel; channels should be used for clarity and correctness, with the lock cost accepted.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The trap answer is 'channels are implemented with atomics, so they are super fast'. The hchan uses a full mutex; only select's randomization and some fast paths avoid locking. Another trap: 'buffered channels are async, so they never block' — they block when the buffer is full (sends) or empty (receives). Candidates who mention hchan's lock field by name and the sudog wait queues demonstrate real runtime knowledge.

interviewGotchas.question: What happens when you send on a closed channel, and why does ranging behave that way?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This is the canonical channel-semantics question — the interviewer wants the close contract and its interaction with range and receive, precisely.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Sending on a closed channel panics — the runtime checks hchan.closed under the channel's lock before enqueuing. Receiving from a closed channel returns immediately with the zero value (and ok=false with the comma-ok form), so a drain loop must not mistake that for a live value. Range (for v := range ch) keeps receiving until the channel is closed, then exits — that is why close(ch) is the broadcast 'no more values' signal for fan-out workers. Double-closing panics. The rule of thumb: only the sender should close, and close should be deferred or placed where all sends are guaranteed done — closing from a receiver races sends and can panic.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'receiving from a closed channel panics'. It does not — receiving is safe (zero value), sending panics. Another trap: 'closing a channel is like a boolean flag, so anyone can do it' — concurrent closers race and the second close panics. Candidates who state the sender-closes contract and the zero-value drain pitfall precisely show they have actually written concurrent Go.
